# A module is completed whole, so a build that imports several of its packages
# needs no second pass, whichever of them it happened to load first.
#
# One package of this module has a directive that fails on purpose. `go generate`
# abandons that package and carries on with the rest, so the module still arrives
# with every other package's generated file.

env GOFLAGS=-mod=mod

# The fetch completes the module. Whether the generators ran here or their
# overlay came from the build cache, the module that arrives is the same, so
# what the fetch PRINTS is not what this asserts.
go mod download example.com/generatedpkgs

exists $GOPATH/pkg/mod/example.com/generatedpkgs@v1.0.0/one/one.gen.go
exists $GOPATH/pkg/mod/example.com/generatedpkgs@v1.0.0/two/two.gen.go
exists $GOPATH/pkg/mod/example.com/generatedpkgs@v1.0.0/three/three.gen.go

# The broken package generated nothing, and nothing it half-wrote reached the
# module either.
! exists $GOPATH/pkg/mod/example.com/generatedpkgs@v1.0.0/broken/broken.gen.go
! exists $GOPATH/pkg/mod/example.com/generatedpkgs@v1.0.0.generate

# Every other package builds, and the directory matches the checksum recorded
# when it was completed.
go build ./both
go build ./usethree
go mod verify

# The package whose generator failed is the only one missing its symbol.
! go build ./usebroken
stderr 'undefined: broken\.Name'

-- go.mod --
module example.com/consumer

go 1.16

require example.com/generatedpkgs v1.0.0
-- both/both.go --
package both

import (
	"example.com/generatedpkgs/one"
	"example.com/generatedpkgs/two"
)

var Names = one.Name() + two.Name()
-- usebroken/usebroken.go --
package usebroken

import "example.com/generatedpkgs/broken"

var Name = broken.Name()
-- usethree/usethree.go --
package usethree

import "example.com/generatedpkgs/three"

var Name = three.Name()
